VISIT TO BROCKVILLE AND DISTRICT BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, it seems right and proper that the House of Commons and the public should be informed of the fact that the leading intellectuals of all political parties in the house spent the week end at Brockville in the county of Leeds, and in other parts of the province of Ontario. Speaking for myself and others, our visit was a great pleasure from every point of view. We enjoyed all the social functions, and gained firsthand knowledge of one of the beauty spots of Ontario. We visited the truly magnificent Thousand islands, the imposing, comfortable and beautiful tourist resorts of the county, and the industries of Brockville, the principal town.
What caught my attention and imagination was the complete cleanliness of the industrial plants, the beauty and tidiness of the outer surroundings, and the spirit of harmony prevailing between employer and employee. The tidy workshops of industry in the town of Brockville were very different from the dirty and miserable places in other large industrial centres of this country where people must toil day and night.
Our thanks and appreciation must go to the genial member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford). He is not here today, because he is attending the graduation of one of his sons from McGill university. I should also like to express our thanks and appreciation to his most amiable wife, to the mayor and aldermen of the civic corporations of Brockville and Gananoque, and the members of the chambers of commerce, for a wonderful time and an educational feast.
I hope and pray that in the future there will be more such visits from the east of Canada to the centre, from the west to the centre, and from the centre to the east and west, in order that members of the house may obtain firsthand knowledge of the wonderful country in which we are privileged to live.

maintopic: RIMOUSKI AND CABANO-VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER  SCOPE OF DEVASTATION

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I should like to report briefly to the house on what I have been able to observe in the course of the trip I made last Thursday and Friday to Rimouski and Cabano, where I visited the victims of the disasters which occurred in those two cities of the lower St. Lawrence.
I left Dorval Thursday morning with the Solicitor General (Mr. Lapointe), and Mr. Leopold Langlois, member for Gaspe, who acted as representative for the hon. member for Rimouski, Mr. Gleason Belzile. Brigadier Jean Allard, commanding officer of the Quebec military district, joined our party in Quebec city.
Perfect weather and visibility permitted us to have an aerial view of the damaged sections of the towns of Cabano and Rimouski, before we landed for our visit to these two interesting industrial centres.
After landing at Mont Joli airport, we were met by Brigadier A. Theriault, member of the federal-provincial commission which is to report on both disasters, and then our party proceeded immediately by motorcar to Rimouski.
We paid our first call to the city hall, where we were greeted by Mayor Victor Lepage. We met the members of the municipal council, the members of the relief committee, the civic department heads, the engineers, architects and technicians, all of whom were there on loan from the federal and provincial governments. We were shown the properties which were destroyed on the cadastral survey of the city. The plan would be to try to rebuild the district which was burned down by making a new cadastral survey which would take into account the views of the owners, engineers, surveyors and town-planners who are all working in very close co-operation. One can easily imagine the difficulty of the problem when one knows that the damaged area does not allow all previous owners to rebuild their homes if they are to be separated by sufficient space to prevent another disaster.

From the city hall, we went to visit the damaged area, where we met the superior of the seminary. As you know, half of the building, not being fireproof, was burned down. Then we met the nuns in charge of the hospital where extension works had been in progress. Unfortunately even in the fireproof section, flames spread through and caused damage. There we also saw the nuns in charge of the home for the aged and of the orphanage, both of which have disappeared; we also met the manager of the Price Company, whose mill was destroyed. At this time of the year, the mill employed between 500 to 600 men. Although the company's plans for the future are not yet determined, it is held that it will shortly be able to provide work for a good many workers.
We have seen the ruins of 359 houses, the destruction of which has left over 2,000 persons homeless.
Approximately one-quarter of the town has disappeared in this terrible fire, not to mention the vast area covered by the plant and lumber yards of the Price Company.
The canteen set up in the arena by the relief committee has operated very well and it still serves between 1,200 to 1,500 meals a day. In the committee's warehouses, we have been able to see great quantities of clothing, furniture, building material and goods of all sorts which were sent to the victims by sympathetic and generous people in Canada and the United States.
Toward the end of the afternoon, we called on the Archbishop of Rimouski, who expressed his gratitude for the sympathy shown to the population of his episcopal See.
Friday, we went to Cabano with the hon. member for Temiscouata, Mr. Jean Francois Pouliot. In that town, we were greeted by Mayor Emilien Morin and Rev. Canon Cyr, parish priest.
One hundred and fifty-nine homes were destroyed in Cabano, which left over 1,000 persons homeless. In Rimouski every victim took refuge elsewhere in the city and in surrounding villages; but it could not be so in Cabano, where close to a third of the village was destroyed and many of the victims still live under tents supplied by the army or other divisions of the dominion and provincial governments.
In Cabano, as well as in Rimouski, the army and Red Cross have performed an admirable task, and nothing was spared to save the victims from hunger and want.
The population of both localities is courageous and optimistic. The sympathy and

help which they have received are appreciated.
In both towns there are clever and enterprising administrators and businessmen who show a great deal of initiative. In Cabano, the manager of the Fraser Company, whose plant has not been destroyed, assured us that normal operations would be resumed this very morning.
I have conveyed to every one the sympathy of the people of Canada and in both places I stated, as I had done in this very house, that upon receipt of the report concerning the nature and extent of each of the two disasters the federal government would take a similar stand with respect to assistance as was taken in the case of the Fraser valley disaster in 1948.
The members of the commission of inquiry into the disasters at Rimouski and Cabano are proceeding with diligence and the government has reason to believe that they will report on the results of their investigation in the near future.

maintopic: RIMOUSKI AND CABANO-VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER  SCOPE OF DEVASTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), I wish to assure him and the government that the good people of my constituency, which adjoins Rimouski, scene of the terrible catastrophe, are entirely at the officials' disposal in order to help cope with this disastrous problem. The Matane civic authorities have already taken the necessary steps to have the home for the aged in that city replace that of Rimouski. The old Matane hospital has been furnished and will be turned over to the nuns whose own building was lost at Rimouski; this hospital, which is quite suitable, will be used to hospitalize the inmates of the home for the aged in Rimouski.
Many of the Rimouski fire victims have already taken refuge in the constituency of Matapedia-Matane. I am also sure that at Lac au Saumon and at Amqui, people are willing to do all that is humanly possible in order to relieve the hardship suffered by the citizens of Rimouski. Government officials are doubtless aware of the efforts that have already been made in this direction and they also realize that the good people of Matane are very anxious to help the fire victims of Rimouski, if only they are given the opportunity to do so.

maintopic: RIMOUSKI AND CABANO-VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER  SCOPE OF DEVASTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the request of my hon. friend from
Rimouski and Cabano Fires Rimouski (Mr. Belzile), who is at present confined to the hospital, I was indeed happy to represent him at Rimouski while accompanying the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Lapointe) on a tour of that stricken area. If I speak today on behalf of my colleague as well as of the people of the constituency of Rimouski, it is to thank publicly the right hon. the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General for this visit, which was as much a token of sympathy as a means of investigation. My fellow citizens of the fire-ravaged town of Rimouski will most certainly have found in this evidence of interest and sympathy on the part of the government a most valuable incentive in the heavy task of reconstruction which now faces them as a result of this disaster.
I know also that the people of Rimouski were deeply moved by the visit paid them yesterday by Their Excellencies the Governor General and Lady Alexander. I am also certain that this expression of sympathy on the part of His Majesty's representative in Canada has been greatly appreciated by these sadly afflicted people.
I also wish to thank the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote), as well as his fellow citizens and constituents, for the generous support and valuable help they gave to the people of Rimouski during and since that disaster.

maintopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 1
speechtext:
Before this motion carries I think the house .should consider the advisability of deferring the date for a week. I am making the suggestion because so many of the committees are sitting at the present time. Some committees have not by any means reached the reporting stage; some of them, in fact, have just begun to sit.
Our experience of the last week or so, when committees were sitting in the afternoon as well as in the morning, indicated the difficulty of hon. members paying attention to the business that was actually before the house. On a number of days last week I made a count of the hon. members in the chamber. I am not blaming hon. members who were out of the chamber, but at times during the week over a hundred members were absent, sitting on committees in the various committee rooms. Committees should be nearer the reporting stage before this motion is passed.
I looked up Hansard of the pre-war years -and this should be considered as a postwar sitting-and this is what I found. In 1935, for example, there were only three morning sittings out of 97 sitting days; in 1936 there were four morning sittings out of 91 sitting days; in 1937 there were nine morning sittings out of 62 sitting days. In 1938 there were only four out of 102; and in 1939, when we were dealing with defence matters because of the international situation that had developed, we did have 20 morning sittings out of 103 sitting days.
Even during the war we did not have a great many morning sittings. In the spring session of 1940 we had 11 morning sittings out of 61 sitting days. In 1941 we had 20 out of 105; in 1942 we had 13 out of 124; in 1943, 14 out of 120.
House of Commons
This is the sixty-sixth day of the session. It seems to me that a motion for morning sittings is premature, both because of the number of days we have sat, and because of the business of the house which has been referred to -committees, which is not completed and which will require a great deal of attention from hon. members.
While we are all anxious that the business of the house shall be completed before the intensely hot weather arrives, because when it is hot it is difficult to give the kind of attention that should be given to the business of the house, I think reconsideration should be given to the date, and I move the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by deleting therefrom the words "June 1" and substituting therefor the words "June 8."
This will give us one more week to complete the committee work, and a chance to attend to the business of the house as well as of the committees. Perhaps the Prime Minister would consider changing the date himself, so that I would not have to press the motion; but I wanted to put it regularly before the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER THURSDAY, JUNE 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it does not seem to me that any reason has been put before the house for this motion; therefore I do not think we should add an amendment calling for morning sittings to start a week from June 1. I am not taking issue with the view expressed as to the undesirability of starting morning sittings at this point, but I do question the possibility that any of the committees will have presented their reports between now and a week from Thursday-
There is strong reason why the motion should not be pressed at this time. A number of extremely important committees are sitting. They are committees dealing with social security, public accounts and a number of other matters that are being examined with a great deal of care. Agriculture is coming up. The national defence committee is in process of considering a very long bill which has been referred to it. At the stage when we are asked to sit at eleven o'clock in the morning, at the same time as all these committees are meeting, a committee appointed with the authority of the government, on motion of the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) to deal with amendments to the elections act, has not yet been called, although the question has been asked several times when it would meet. If there has been any delay in the convening of these committees then the responsibility for that delay must be fully

House of Commons
assumed by the government and those charged with the responsibility of directing the business of the house.
Members on the government side, as on this side, who have been attending these committees have been showing a commendable desire, in a great many of the committee activities-in fact, in most of them-to produce useful results and to facilitate the business of the house. I do not think it is possible for members who are sitting on several committees-and their number involves an actual majority of the members of the house-to give consideration to the business of those committees and also to give proper consideration to the business before the house.
No matter what any member may feel about the time that may have been devoted to the discussion of any particular subject, it should be remembered that we have not disposed of the estimates of a single department, that we have dealt with only a few departments, and that the fundamentally important business of the House of Commons, which is the provision of money for the public business, still has to be dealt with.
Particularly in view of the reluctance to set up a committee on estimates, and the invitation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to examine the estimates carefully-which invitation, I may say, will be accepted-I do submit through you, Mr. Speaker, that this motion is premature. If it is intended that the committees shall have the opportunity to deal with their very important business as they should, this motion should not be pressed but rather should stand until there is some opportunity to see how rapidly the committees can proceed with their work.
Let us recall the criticism that there has been no attempt made fully to examine all the facts. May I say that with a committee on estimates sitting there would be an opportunity to do that. But if there is an attempt to proceed at the same time both in the house and in committees, and it is not humanly possible for members to deal adequately with all these activities, then there may well be justification for the suggestion that there has not been afforded a proper opportunity to go into such questions as social security, public accounts, agriculture, and all these other matters which are under consideration-to say nothing of the very important committee moved by a minister of the crown to deal with amendments to the elections act and certain recommendations which have been made.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (for ihe Minister of Fisheries) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON, FEBRUARY 8, 1949
speechtext: That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the ratification, without reservation. of the .international convention for the northwest Atlantic fisheries, signed in Washington on February 8. 1949, but subject to the observation that ratification by Canada of the convention extends to Newfoundland and that any claims Canada may have in regard to the limits of territorial waters or to the jurisdiction over fisheries, particularly as a result of the entry of Newfoundland into confederation, will not be prejudiced, and that this house do approve same.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MacNaught (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON, FEBRUARY 8, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the northwest Atlantic area has been, during several centuries, an important fishing ground for the nationals of North American and western and southern European countries. Recognizing the need for scientific investigation and protection of the fishery resources of this area, Canada, the United States of America, Great Britain, Newfoundland, France, Spain, Portugal, Iceland, Denmark, Norway, and Italy signed the international convention for the northwest Atlantic fisheries following a conference in Washington in February, 1949.
The convention provides for the establishment of a commission on which all contracting governments will be represented, and separate panels with jurisdiction over defined sub-areas in which governments with particular fishing interests will have representations. The over-all area covered by the convention is divided into five sub-areas. These areas generally cover the waters off the west coast of Greenland, and the waters off the coasts of Labrador, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the New England states of the United States. Provision is made in the convention to safeguard any claims to territorial waters, or jurisdiction over the fisheries of the contracting parties.
The primary functions of the commission under the convention will be to collect, collate and disseminate scientific information on international fisheries in the convention area. The commission has no regulatory powers, but any panel may transmit, through the commission to the governments represented on
294S

Halibut Fishery
such panel, recommendations for joint action of a regulatory nature in respect of those stocks of fish that support international fisheries.
The permanent seat of the commission will be in North America at a place to be determined by the commission. The convention will enter into force upon ratification by any four signatory governments. The convention has now been ratified by Great Britain, Iceland and the United States. It would accordingly come into force upon deposit of the instrument of ratification by Canada.
At the Washington conference which adopted the convention, Newfoundland was represented by a separate delegation, .and the convention was signed "for His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and the government of Newfoundland in respect of Newfoundland." The United Kingdom government, in depositing their instrument of ratification, drew attention to the fact that their ratification did not include ratification in respect of Newfoundland. When the Canadian government ratifies this convention an observation will be attached to our instrument of ratification, making clear that the ratification covers Newfoundland, and pointing out that the provision in the convention safeguarding any claims to territorial waters has taken a broader meaning as far as the Canadian government is concerned since Newfoundland has been united with Canada. This observation will therefore assert that the Canadian ratification is on the basis that the provision referred to above entirely protects all claims to territorial waters and jurisdiction over fisheries, particularly as a result of the alteration in the Canadian boundaries that has taken place by the joining of the tenth province.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION FOR EXTENSION OF PACIFIC COAST PORT PRIVILEGES SIGNED AT OTTAWA, MARCH 24, 1950
speechtext: That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the ratification, without reservation, of the convention for the extension of port privileges to halibut fishing vessels on the Pacific coasts of the United States of America and Canada, signed at Ottawa on March 24, 1950, and that this house do approve same.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MacNaughf (Parliameniary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION FOR EXTENSION OF PACIFIC COAST PORT PRIVILEGES SIGNED AT OTTAWA, MARCH 24, 1950
speechtext:
The
convention provides for reciprocal port privileges to be granted to halibut fishing [Mr. MacNaught.l
vessels of Canada and the United States in the ports on the Pacific coasts of each country. The privileges are:
(1)	to land their catches of halibut and sablefish without the payment of duties and
(a)	sell them locally on payment of the applicable customs duty;
(b)	transship them in bond under customs supervision to any part of either country; or
(c)	sell them in bond for export; and
(2)	to obtain supplies, repairs and equipment, subject to compliance with applicable customs and navigation laws of either country.
These privileges which have been granted heretofore on an annual basis by special legislation will now be made available to the halibut fishermen of both countries on a continuing basis, so that in advance of the fishing season the fishing industry will be assured of the privileges that will be available.
In addition, the convention will alter the present practice in one other respect. It will extend the reciprocal port privileges to Canadian halibut vessels in ports of the United States proper, whereas at present these privileges are granted only in the ports of Alaska.
The convention will continue for an indefinite time, but can be terminated by either government upon 12 months' notice.
A recent survey of the opinion of the fishing industry on the Pacific coast indicated general support in favour of the treaty.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION FOR EXTENSION OF PACIFIC COAST PORT PRIVILEGES SIGNED AT OTTAWA, MARCH 24, 1950
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly in support of this resolution providing for the adoption of the treaty which deals with reciprocal port privileges for fishermen of the Pacific coast. But before dealing with the treaty itself, may I be permitted to make one other observation. This convention was signed on March 24 last for Canada by R. W. Mayhew and for the United States of America by the late Laurence A. Steinhardt. I wish to take just a moment to pay my little tribute to that outstanding gentleman, one of whose last official acts was the signing of this convention. We on the Pacific coast had the pleasure of meeting His Excellency and discussing with him several matters relative to fishing, Alaska and other subjects; and I know that I am expressing the feelings of all my people who met him when I say how deeply we regret his loss.
With reference to the convention itself, for the fishing people of my district I welcome this convention. As a Canadian, I welcome it as just another of the many examples of good neighbourliness between ourselves and

the United States. As has been said, this convention is similar to an agreement already in force applicable to British Columbia and Alaska ports; but it extends the operation of the agreement to the Pacific coast ports of the United States proper. I hope that this convention will be lived up to fully by both countries; and it is just on that point that I want to take a minute or two of the time of the house.
Articles I and II are the operative articles. They are similar except that article I refers to the privileges we are granting to American vessels and article II refers to the privileges of Canadian vessels in American ports.
Article II reads as follows:
Fishing vessels of Canada engaged in the north Pacific halibut fishery only shall, subject to compliance with applicable customs and navigation laws of the United States of America, have the privileges, in the ports of entry of the United States of America:
(1)	To land their catches of halibut and sablefish without the payment of duties and
(a)	sell them locally on payment of the applicable customs duty;
(b)	transship them in bond under customs supervision to any port of Canada; or
(c)	sell them in bond for export; and
(2)	To obtain supplies, repairs and equipment.
I wish particularly to draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to those words "halibut fishery only" which appear in the opening lines of the article. I know that later on it grants the privileges of landing halibut and sablefish. I am not for one moment suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that there was anything but the best of good faith on the part both of the United States and of Canada when this convention was negotiated and signed. But customs officers, both American and Canadian, cannot all be experts on fish nor experts in reading legal documents. Any customs officer or port official, suddenly and for the first time faced with a case under this treaty, might quite easily glance at these words "halibut fishery only" and come to the conclusion that the treaty applies to halibut only. Like myself, he might not know what sablefish includes. He might not know that it included cod.
This is not just a theoretical fear. About two years ago a case occurred in connection with this treaty before it was extended beyond Alaska. My recollection of that case is that a Canadian vessel put into the port of Sitka and was refused permission to land ten thousand pounds of cod, but she was partly disabled and unable to proceed. The matter was taken up with the appropriate authorities; but fresh cod does not remain fresh cod while awaiting the outcome of negotiations between Washington and Ottawa.
International Labour Organization Eventually, I understand, instructions were issued pointing out to the Alaska customs officials that their decision was in error. But in the meantime the cod had had to be dumped, a total loss. My request to the parliamentary assistant is that the Department of Fisheries, in conjunction with the Department of External Affairs, or whatever other authorities are proper, shall make absolutely certain that the customs and port officials will know just what this convention does mean. Inasmuch as fish, as I have said, is such a perishable product, it is essential that these officers be fully briefed before any occasion arises to use the advantages of the treaty. Before this short debate is concluded, when he closes it, I would ask the parliamentary assistant to give us an assurance on that point.	.

subtopic: APPROVAL OP EMPLOYMENT SERVICE CONVENTION ADOPTED AT SAN FRANCISCO, JULY 9, 1948

speakeroldname: Hon. Humphrey Mitchell (Minister of Labour) moved:
subtopic: APPROVAL OP EMPLOYMENT SERVICE CONVENTION ADOPTED AT SAN FRANCISCO, JULY 9, 1948
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of convention No. 88, employment service convention, 1948, which was adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization at its thirty-first session at San Francisco on the ninth day of July, 1948, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: The purpose of this resolution is to obtain the approval by parliament of an international labour convention passed by the general conference of the international labour organization at San Francisco at its thirty-first session in June, 1948. This convention, No. 88, is designated the employment service convention, 1948. Copies of the text have been distributed to hon. members. Upon approval of its terms by parliament, the government proposes to proceed to the ratification of the convention.
Convention No. 88 provides that each member state ratifying the convention shall maintain a free public employment service, consisting of a national system of employment offices under the jurisdiction of a national authority. The duty of the employment service shall be to ensure the best possible organization of the labour market, in co-operation with other public and private bodies concerned. Co-operation of employers and workers shall be secured through national, regional and local advisory committees.

International Labour Organization
The organization of the employment service shall be so arranged as to assist workers to find suitable employment and to assist employers to find suitable workers on a voluntary basis. It shall also facilitate the movement of workers to areas with suitable employment opportunities, shall collect and make available information on the employment market, co-operate in the administration of unemployment insurance and other measures for the relief of the unemployed, assist in social and economic planning to ensure a favourable employment situation, and by vocational guidance endeavour to meet adequately the needs of particular categories of persons, such as disabled persons and young persons.
The Canadian representatives at the San Francisco conference voted for the approval of this convention.
It will be evident, I think, to all hon. members that Canada is already in full compliance with the provisions of the convention. Under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, we have established and are operating a national employment service in conjunction with the unemployment insurance provisions of the act. The nature and standards of service provided by the national employment service under the act are certainly at least as high and as complete as those laid down in the convention.
The opinion of the law officers of the crown is that it is within the legislative competence of parliament to give effect to this convention, and no new legislation is required for this purpose.
The convention has already been ratified by the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden and Bulgaria.
In my opinion, Canada should proceed to the ratification of this convention for the reason that in the provision and operation of our national employment service we have given effect to the convention, and to indicate Canada's approval of its objectives and thus to give leadership and support to higher international labour standards, and for the establishment of similar services in other countries.
Perhaps I should explain just what obligations follow upon the ratification of an international labour organization convention by a member state. When the formal ratification has been communicated to the director general of the international labour organization, the ratifying state is required to take such action as may still be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the convention within the state by the enactment of legislation or otherwise, if this has not already been done.

Each of the states ratifying the convention agrees to make periodic reports to the international labour office on the measures which it has taken to give effect to the provisions of the convention. In short, a member state ratifying a convention undertakes an obligation that the provisions of the convention shall be given continuing effect in that its legislation and practice on the subject are on a level at least as high as the standards set by the provisions of the particular convention.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say. In fact, I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), namely, that we regard the international labour organization as one of the most valuable pieces of international machinery established thus far. It has survived the test of a good many years as an international organization. We feel, too, that the means whereby the ILO works is a very useful and practical one, namely, that of having conventions considered and ratified at ILO conferences, following which that ratification is confirmed by the various countries represented.
This particular convention concerning employment services does seem to be one that is highly desirable to be laid down as a minimum for all countries that belong to the international labour organization. I think we would agree that Canada has gone at least some distance in pursuit of the principles laid down in this convention.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of those motions for which there is only one stage of debate. When this motion carries, that is the end of it so far as this house is concerned. But the minister can close the debate, and I would like, if I may, to ask a couple of questions-rhetorically-and perchance the minister would be good enough to answer them. My first question is this: First of all, does the government feel that there are any further steps that it will have to take, after it deposits the ratification of this convention, to make sure that Canada is


living up to all of the terms of this convention? My second question is: Are there any outstanding ILO conventions which Canada has not yet ratified?

subtopic: APPROVAL OP EMPLOYMENT SERVICE CONVENTION ADOPTED AT SAN FRANCISCO, JULY 9, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am not so enthusiastic about the ratification of this convention as some other hon. members seem to be, although I am not going to object seriously to it. I have a background which perhaps largely governs my thinking, and I must confess that I always look a little askance at the possibility of entangling ourselves with international organizations. I know that today civilization has reached a place where no nation lives unto itself. Nevertheless the tendency all around us in these days is to give to some outside body authority which belongs to us over our own affairs. I have never been able to bring myself to believe that is a wise move at any time.
While I am desirous that all nations should co-operate one with another, I believe we are headed for trouble if we put authority in the hands of any international body which would in any way eventually impose its will upon any individual nation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, paying some little attention to this particular convention, I must say that I am disappointed we did not have this printed or mimeographed document presented to us before. It was lying on our desks when we came here at three o'clock. The motion to adopt it was moved just a few moments ago. Between three o'clock and four-thirty our minds have been engaged in other matters. What opportunity have we had, as members of parliament, to read this convention in the last hour and a half? Yet we are now called upon as the parliament of Canada to ratify it.
I believe this could have been done tomorrow or on a subsequent day, and that a convention of this kind might well have been sent to the committee on industrial relations for further study. As the convention is not greatly involved, perhaps it has been considered unnecessary to send it to that committee. However, there may be underlying it certain principles a committee would have had an opportunity to consider in greater detail than can be expected in this house at the present time.
As I have glanced at it here and there in the last short while, it appears to me that Canada has already gone as far as this convention would go in respect of the management of our own labour problems. We have
, 1950
International Labour Organization done this through the medium of the various employment offices across the country, and have been doing it for some years. In my view those employment offices have been doing a good job. While I have been in touch with only one or two of them, I have no fault to find, and would commend them.
I believe I am not far wrong when I say that at the international labour conference held at San Francisco they spent a great deal of time and energy, and must have spent a large sum of money, in attempting to do something Canada has already done. That is the way I feel about it; and there is no reason in the world why any other nation could not have done the same thing without necessarily subscribing to a convention of this kind. Those are my personal feelings in the matter.
As I look through the convention, about the only feature of an international nature I can find is that which appears at page 2, as article VI (b) (iv), which refers to facilitating the movement of workers from one country to another, as approved by the governments concerned. I had to read all the way down to that sentence to learn what the international aspect was. Up to that point it described only something we have already done.
I call the attention of the house to article V on page 2 which states:
The general policy of the unemployment service in regard to referral of workers to available employment shall be developed after consultation of representatives of employers and workers through the advisory committees provided for in article IV.
As I read that, I thought I had never
seen the word referral before. I do not claim to be a grammarian-indeed, sometimes I think I murder the King's English- but in this instance I called for the dictionary that is usually kept on the Clerk's table. It is the Concise Oxford Dictionary, and I find it does not contain the word referral. Therefore I am still at a loss to know what it means. I fancy it is a word which has been cleverly coined, and that its actual meaning is to transfer. When we talk about the transfer of workers it connotes to us something that might be dangerous in a free country like Canada.
When it comes to matters of employment, I believe we must view them from the standpoint of the obvious fact that we are living in a civilization moving at such a rapid pace that we have passed the day when we can think and talk in terms of full employment. Therefore we have to devise other means and think of things in terms other than those of simply putting everybody to work. Governments will be faced with almost insurmountable difficulties-I was going to say

International Labour Organization impossibilities-in an age such as that in which we live, where we have technological advances which are continually putting people out of work, an age in which we encourage technological advancement. We do that on the one hand, and then on the other we talk in terms of full employment.
* I remember a lobbyist coming to my office some few years ago and asking me a number of questions. I felt I should have been the one asking the questions, but it was he who began the questioning by asking, "Do you believe in full employment, Mr. Hansell?" "Well," I said, "you tell me what you mean by full employment. Define your term." I continued, "When I was a boy my father used to get up with the chickens, work hard all day, and perhaps go to bed at dusk. He did that six days a week. I suggest to you that that would be full employment. Is that what you mean?" Oh no, he did not mean that. Labour organizations usually work eight hours a day, and he fancied that eight hours a day for six days a week would be full employment. I said, "No, I do not believe in that sort of full employment. I believe in six hours a day; I believe in four hours a day. What do you have to say to that?" He said, "Well, that would be very nice if we as workers could get by with working four or six hours a day, but I am afraid we would not be able to earn enough money working that number of hours." I said, "That depends on how much an hour you are getting." He said to me, "Well, of course, a man getting $1 an hour and working eight hours a day would get $8 a day, and if he were only working four hours he would only get $4 a day." I said, "Yes, that is a very profound observation." He said that he would not be able to live on that. I said, "Suppose the whole industrial machinery' of the country working four hours a day should produce an overabundance of things. What then? If there were a possibility of augmenting your wages in some other way in order that you might have the advantage of the great production of the nation, would that not do?" He said, "I suppose it would, but is there any way that can be done?" I said, "I will tell you what to do. You call on Mr. King and ask him if he has a way he can suggest. Then after that call on Mr. Bracken and ask him if he has any way in which to handle a thing like that. When you are through with him call on Mr. Coldwell and ask him if he has any way of overcoming that difficulty. When you find they have no way then come back to me and we will talk a little further about it."

I have not seen the gentleman since but I think I can draw some rather correct conclusions. Returning to the document, I should like to suggest-and I say this purely on my own responsibility-that after the international labour organization has brought industry and labour into the position of a socialist state they will have all the stage work done for Uncle Joe. I see in this document something respecting the transfer of workers. That is exactly what Stalin would like us to have. I see no difficulty in the way of each country being able to run its own industrial organization in a co-operative way with one country learning from another. My profound conclusion is that the more we tie our hands to an international authority the less authority we shall have over the management of our own affairs.
Not so long ago we listened in the house to the pipe lines debate which took a long time to finish. The press and others referred to it as a filibuster. I am not debating that now, but there was one note sounded in that debate, and I have no objection to its being sounded." The view was expressed that we were taking our natural resources and giving them away to another nation. In the first place we were not giving them away. If we had any natural resources to dispose of we were selling them. That is one place where a mistake was made in the phraseology because we were not giving anything away. In some quarters of the house the measures were vigorously opposed because, so they said, we were giving away some of our natural resources. It was said that we must not do that, but when it comes to international organizations we can give away our freedom as fast as you like, and no objection is raised to that. I would rather sell our natural resources to another nation than give away some of our sovereignty, thus rendering us less free to manage our own affairs.
I simply warn of the danger of entangling ourselves with international organizations which will have the effect of outside authorities telling us how to run our own business and we shall not be able to tell them to mind their own business. That is the way I feel about these questions. As I said before, I see nothing particularly harmful in this convention, because I think we are several jumps ahead of it. In Canada we have already established our local employment offices that are able to do a good job. Let other nations take a leaf from the management of our affairs and do likewise.

subtopic: APPROVAL OP EMPLOYMENT SERVICE CONVENTION ADOPTED AT SAN FRANCISCO, JULY 9, 1948
speechtext:
The international labour office is the oldest international organization in existence today. It was founded in 1919 in the city of Washington, U.S.A. I might point out to my hon. friend that at the Paris peace conference of 1918, under the chairmanship of Sir Robert Borden, the principles of this organization were enunciated, and eventually the ILO was established in Washington the following year. If I remember rightly Senator Robertson was one of the official delegates at that time. I forget the others, though I knew them quite well.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) spoke of national sovereignty. I do not think anyone in this house is going to suggest that the sovereignty of this nation be given up to any other nation. This is merely a declaration, to establish a principle. I would point out also that this is a tripartite organization, consisting of representatives of employers, employees and the governments of the respective countries; and I believe that
International Labour Organization in a broad and general way it has had a tremendous influence on what might be called the more backward countries of the world, in raising the standard of employment conditions and other things we have taken for granted in this country down through the years. I think perhaps it has contributed more than any other international organization, whether it be political, financial'or anything else. I am not going to get into an argument about the financial aspect, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod. This is not the time or place for that debate.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked whether any changes would be made to fit our system into this convention. I believe I made it clear in my opening statement that to my knowledge we are living up to all the provisions of the convention, and the hon. member may rest assured that from time to time the government will endeavour to increase the efficiency of the employment service of this country. As Canadians I think we can be proud of the speedy development of that organization. I lived through the agitation for it for thirty years, when the labour organizations of this country were violently opposing the maintenance of fee-charging employment agencies. Those of us who were close to the situation during those days know something of what that practice did to the working people of this country. This afternoon we have heard representatives of every party in the house, including the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), agree that this convention should be adopted, so that would seem to be the thought of every party here.
My hon. friend asked why this resolution was not introduced last year. That was not done for the simple reason that last year we had a situation somewhat similar to the situation developing this year. There is a limit to human endurance. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre smiles. That is the easiest thing in the world to do when you have no responsibility. Let me remind the hon. member that it costs more than $6,000 for every minute this house is in operation. I wish someone who has more leisure than I would count the time some hon. members have taken up in this house and multiply it by six thousand. I am a great believer in the British way of discussion. I think a better speech can be made in ten minutes than in forty minutes, and if

International Labour Organization you cannot say all you know about a subject in twenty minutes you do not know anything about it. The hon. member for Macleod was speaking about long words, and I forget the one he used; but I am a great believer in basic English. When you are in a jam, use a long word to get yourself out of it. No one will understand it, including yourself.
Then I was asked why this document had not been circulated before this. Well, it is a public document, and I believe the basic principles were carried in the Labour Gazette. As an afterthought it occurred to me that it might be circulated to hon. members today.
1 do not believe it would have made any difference if it had been circulated earlier, because we are all agreed upon the soundness of the principles under discussion. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked what interest the government had taken in the I.L.O. As a federal parliament we have so far approved twelve conventions. Anyone who has followed the work of the I.L.O. closely knows the difficulties that occur in what we call a federal state. They have the same problems in the United States, Australia, and other countries in connection with the approval of these conventions. In the United States and Canada hours and wages, for instance, come under the jurisdiction of the state and provincial governments. In Australia there is also divided authority on labour relations, and the same might be said of South Africa. There is one reason we have not approved as many conventions on paper as some other countries. Anything works on paper, but I like to see a plan in operation day after day. I seem to recall that prior to the last war the nation that had adopted the most conventions at the I.L.O. was Roumania, but I do not hear of anyone in Canada wanting to live in Roumania. I have some knowledge of many Roumanians who want to come to Canada, and I do not blame them. I believe the adoption of any policy by a deliberative assembly like this house should be based upon the practical application,of that policy to the lives of the people to whom we are responsible.
I do not believe there is much more I can say, except to remind hon. members that the
I.L.O. will be in session next month in Geneva. I wish I could be there; I hear someone say they wish they could see me there. In all my years as Minister of Labour I have not attended a convention of the I.L.O. outside this country. Mine is a busy department, as hon. members know, and I have never had that opportunity. Some day I would like to attend a meeting of the I.L.O. in Geneva, representative as it is of more than fifty nations and making, as it does, a great

contribution to the lives of the men and women who work on the farms, in the mines, in the industry and commerce of the countries affiliated with it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO APPEALS TO TARIFF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, section 2 proposes to repeal three provisions of the present act. It proposes to repeal section 43(3), section 43A in its entirety, and section 47(4). In what I have to say I have no quarrel with the proposal to repeal section 43A or section 47(4), but I do submit that the proposal to repeal section 43(3) is unfortunate, and would be a retrograde step.
The purpose or effect of section 43(3) is to confer a right of appeal to the tariff board from certain decisions of the minister under the Customs Act. The other provisions of that section, namely, subsections 1 and 2, empower the minister to fix arbitrary values in certain cases. The effect of subsection 3 of section 43 is to confer a right of appeal from such decisions of the minister. The purpose of clause 2 of the bill, that is the part of it I am now discussing, is to eliminate in its entirety the right of appeal from the decision of the minister to the tariff board. I submit that there is no reason for eliminating that right of appeal.
The jurisdiction of the tariff board on such appeals is limited to confirming or lowering the artificial value fixed by the minister under
Customs Act
an earlier subsection than section 43. It cannot raise such value. If one looks at the explanatory note opposite section 2 of the bill, one finds the following words:
Subsection 3 of section 43 was enacted in 1937 to implement a trade agreement with the United' States which is no longer in effect.
Whether or not that explanation is correct, sir, in so far as it goes it is only an explanation as to how this section came into the act in the first place. I do not know whether that was the only circumstance that led parliament to enact section 43(3) in 1937, but I do know that, the section being in the act, there is nothing in the explanatory note that calls for its repeal. We are simply told that the circumstances which called the section into being in 1937 have passed, that particular agreement with the United States being no longer in effect. This section giving the right of appeal to the tariff board is a sound remedial provision, and no reason for its repeal has been given.
This right of appeal was exercised last year in one case, and I might inform the committee that in that case the tariff board upset the decision of the minister by reducing the amount of the artificial valuation which the minister had fixed under the powers conferred in the earlier subsections of section 43.
In my submission, sir, this question is not affected in the least by the Geneva agreement. If we were dealing with any question in relation to the Geneva agreement, the whole of section 43, including the two earlier subsections, would be immediately called into question under the existing protocol of provisional application of the Geneva agreement which Canada has signed. The provisions of part II of the agreement need only be applied "to the fullest extent not inconsistent with existing legislation." This is such existing legislation. Article VII, subsection 2(a), of the Geneva agreement reads as follows:
The value for customs purposes of imported merchandise should be based on the actual value of the imported merchandise on which duty is assessed, or of like merchandise, and should not be based on the value of merchandise of national origin or on arbitrary or fictitious values.
There is nothing in the explanatory note to indicate that that was in the mind of the draftsman of this section of the bill. If it were, if that is to be the reason given for bringing forward this legislation, I have to say that in the first place the article is not fully in effect because of the existing protocol of provisional application to which I have referred. In the second place even if it were being applied as to the signatories of the Geneva agreement, it certainly would have

Customs Act
no application to any of the other countries in the world. It happens to have been one of those other countries whose exports to Canada were involved in that case to which I referred as having been appealed to the tariff board from the minister's decision last year.
There are other nations that would be affected by this, and what will be the effect if we legislate as proposed here? Those affected by the decisions of the minister under the earlier subsections of section 43 will be deprived of the right of appeal to the tariff board. In my submission there is no reason at all for depriving any such person of the salutary right of appeal to the tariff board. Surely we believe in the tariff board. It is an existing institution under existing legislation of this parliament. According to today's order paper there is to be an amendment introduced to the Tariff Board Act dealing with the procedure before the tariff board. The tariff board is surely here to stay. Then why should we deprive persons who are affected by decisions of the minister in fixing an artificial value on imports of their right to appeal to the tariff board? If the tariff board is a salutary institution, and if this right of appeal to the board from decisions of the minister is a salutary institution, I submit there is no occasion whatsoever for repealing section 43, subsection 3, of the Customs Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO APPEALS TO TARIFF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
This bill is a Department of National Revenue bill, not a Department of Finance bill. The point which the hon. member for Eglinton was attempting to make would be a good one if it were an appeal from a ruling of the department; that is, the deputy minister. Perhaps I should say a few words in general explanation to hon. members about the purpose of this particular section of the customs bill.
The present section 43 of the Customs Act gives the Minister of National Revenue the power to put a quite arbitrary value on the imports of goods if it is thought that the goods are being dumped and the effect is going to be prejudicial to the manufacturers of Canada. On that artificial value of course is then levied the ad valorem rate of duty and whatever dumping duty would apply. As the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out, the Geneva agreements removed that type of artificial fixing of prices from our tax structure as it affects those countries signatory to the Geneva trade agreements. It is, however, still necessary to have such a protection amongst those countries which did not, either by choice or for other reasons, take part in the Geneva agreements. I think perhaps I should give a list of the countries in connection with whose trade we still think it is 
necessary for Canadian industry to have this protection. They are Abyssinia, Afghanistan, Anglo-Egyptian Soudan, Arabia, Bulgaria, Egypt, the eastern zone of Germany, Honduras, Hungary, Iran, Iraq, Japan, Peru, Roumania, Russia and Siam. It is not the deputy minister of national revenue-that is, the department-who actually assesses or fixes this arbitrary value as a matter of departmental administration. It is a serious step to put on such a value, and so is a matter of government policy. The matter is first of all discussed in council, and the governor in council passes an enabling order specifying, first of all, the goods and secondly the country of origin. Then under this authority the Minister of National Revenue issues a specific order fixing the arbitrary price which is going to be set on the goods in question. This section of the bill now does remove the right of appeal to the tariff board from such an action by the minister. We still have that full right of appeal from departmental rulings, and we are extending the field of these appeals to include other interested parties.
There is a great difference between an appeal to the tariff board from a departmental ruling by the deputy minister of customs and excise and an appeal to the tariff board from a matter which has been discussed by council, which has been followed up by an order in council setting out government policy and then by a specific order from the minister. It puts the tariff board in an impossible position to be asked to rule in the latter circumstances; and because of that, this change is being made. This legislation now affects only those countries which I have listed, and will be used only as a protection for Canadian industry against dumping at unfair prices by producers of those countries.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO APPEALS TO TARIFF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
I thank the parliamentary
assistant for his statement because I think that everything he has said has strengthened the case I am putting before the committee for retention of the existing right of appeal under section 43, subsection 3. Let us be quite clear about this. In the first place, Mr. Chairman, we are not discussing the power given to the minister to set an arbitrary or fictitious value for customs or anti-dumping purposes. These provisions are contained in the earlier subsections of this section. No one is proposing in any degree to interfere with those. Those stand and they do not come into this discussion in any way whatever. What we are discussing, and the one question before the committee now, is whether an existing right of appeal to the tariff board against such decisions should be eliminated.

The parliamentary assistant complained that we are putting the tariff board in an impossible position by retaining this right of appeal to them from a decision of the minister. That is a far-fetched argument to put before this committee when we know that last year, when an appeal was taken, under this subsection, to the tariff board, they upset the decision of the minister. What is so impossible about that? Apparently the tariff board is not worried about the embarrassment of sitting on an appeal from decisions of the minister under the earlier subsections of section 43. They felt quite at liberty in that case to upset the decision of the minister.
I think it is clear that what is bothering somebody here is not a question of the impossibility of the position of the tariff board. Somebody apparently feels that the minister's decisions are so infallible that they should not be subject to appeal. That, Mr. Chairman, is a theory that I cannot hold with at all. The minister, in exercising the powers given to him under this and other sections, is proceeding on an administrative basis, surely; and so far as he is exercising judgment, surely it is not unreasonable that that judgment should be open to appeal to a tariff board in which we all believe. If there was anything in this situation that demeaned the minister in, exercising his right to make decisions under section 43, subsections 1 and 2, then this demeaning provision has existed for the last thirteen years in legislation of this parliament. Surely it is not going to demean unduly the minister and his prerogatives to allow that legislation to continue on the statute books.
It is sound legislation to protect a right of appeal to be taken to the tariff board in a situation of this kind. If you take away this right of appeal, you are saying in effect that there should be no right of appeal from a decision of the minister in a case of this kind, that the minister's judgment is final, and that he is infallible. As long as we have humans exercising these powers of judgment, there are bound to be mistakes, as was shown last year. Let us not take away from those affected a right of appeal in legislation in remedial form in this respect. Why take away from people a right they have today, which cannot be abused, and which does not hurt the government, but which exists and gives some protection to those who are affected by it?
Mr. Chairman, I move:
That clause 2 of the said bill be amended by striking out the words "subsection three of section forty-three of the said act as enacted by section six of chapter nineteen of the statutes of 1936.
Tariff Board Act

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) suggests that I say a word by way of explanation. I will make it very brief because the explanatory matter published opposite each section of the bill is pretty lucid. The bill comes from the Senate, which has given it careful consideration. It represents the annual amendments to the Criminal Code which the government recommends to the house at this session. In so far as second reading is concerned, the bill deals with fourteen separate matters which have little in common. There is no principle common to them all, and the only thing that can be said to bind them together in the one bill is that they all have to do with amendments to the Criminal Code, an act of a very comprehensive nature. Therefore I think we shall make much better progress if I just say these few words on second reading and then go into committee where, if further explanations are desired by hon. members with regard to any of the amendments, I shall be glad to provide them if I can.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BREAKING AND ENTERING, FORGERY, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so far as the actual amendments are concerned, with two exceptions they cover amendments that are technical or procedural. The minister having said that the bill represents all the amendments to the Criminal Code the government intends to introduce at this session, it becomes necessary for me to refer to a number of matters having to do with the administration of the criminal law. I regret that some of the suggestions I am about to make have not found their way into the amendments that are being introduced on this occasion by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). I am sure he will agree with me that there is nothing more important than that the criminal law should be maintained and kept up to date. To that end the criminal law amendment commission has been sitting since January 1949. It is charged with the responsibility of recommending such revisions and changes in the criminal law as are deemed necessary by the members of that commission under the distinguished chairmanship of Chief Justice Martin of the Saskatchewan court of appeal.
When I say enforcement of the criminal law is of major importance, and I notice the changes that are made with regard to firearms, what has taken place within the last two days in the city of Montreal underlines the necessity for agencies of the crown to do everything possible to minimize the use of firearms, particularly revolvers, pistols and other such weapons. Indeed there is an article in tonight's paper indicating that a special reward has been offered by the Canadian Bankers Association in the case of the gunman who killed Royal Canadian Mounted Police constable Alexander Gam-man during an attempted hold-up a few days ago in that city. The minister being in fact the titular head of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I suggest to him that no person should be allowed to wander about our country with even the slightest possibility of immunity from arrest without all agencies of the crown and private citizens doing everything they can to ensure his apprehension.
I have referred to a Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer killed in the discharge of his duty. I am sure that the country as a whole would approve of the minister, as head of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, offering an additional reward to that already offered by the Canadian Bankers Association with a view to showing all lawbreakers or potential lawbreakers that the murder of an officer of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shall not go unpunished if agencies of law and civilian organizations can prevent it.

I am not allowed to deal with the various sections of the bill on the motion for second reading, and as the. minister said they can be dealt with in committee. Nevertheless there are one or two things to which I should like to draw his attention. There are certain changes that should be made, and parliament should not wait to make them until the criminal law amendment commission reports. The first one has to do with the provision of the law as it now stands, that in so far as money penalties are concerned the alternative is imprisonment. I have known, as I am sure the Minister of Justice and other legal members of the house also have, of cases where, because an individual was poor and unable to pay his fine, the price of poverty has been a passport to imprisonment. That should not be. If the offence committed merits no more than a fine the pecuniary inability of the accused to pay it should not place him in a position where the stigma of imprisonment hangs over him, and is indeed so often imposed. From experience I know there are many magistrates who, in the enforcement of the law, extend the time for payment, and are often criticized for doing so by the agencies that appoint them.
I feel the time has come in Canada to follow the reform that has been made in this regard in the United Kingdom where a person no longer is imprisoned for failure to pay a fine when he is unable to do so. I also feel that an amendment might be introduced to provide for instalment payments under the law to the end that this injustice will be removed.
Then I come to one further matter. It has to do with respect for the law, because after all the criminal law depends for its enforcement on the respect people have for it. Nothing has done more harm to the enforcement of law in our country than the flagrant flouting of the law on the part of the Sons of Freedom. They have placed themselves above the law, which they regard as simply a means of attaining martyrdom. They commit the most serious offences with the excuse that they are motivated by religious considerations.
This is the first opportunity I have had to pass on a suggestion to the minister. I understand that a commission has been set up in British Columbia to look into the matter and determine what course should be followed. One thing is certain; something must be done. These people cannot be permitted to continue to commit crimes, including arson, at their least whim with impunity under the pretence that they are indeed acting under a religious impulse. I have no interest in the
Criminal Code
name I place before the minister now in connection with that commission. I know something of the influence this gentleman has on Doukhobors who would break our law, and I know that no Anglo-Saxon has had as much experience with these people. I refer to James Wright of Saskatoon, the author of "Slava Bohu", an outstanding book of a few years ago relating to Doukhobors. I know of no one who understands the temperament of the Sons of Freedom as he does, or who has as much influence with them. I must add that he has no particular political qualifications for the position, for he belongs neither to the party of my hon. friend the minister nor to the party to which I belong. His great qualification is his understanding of the problem. He is an authority on the Doukhobors, and in particular on the Sons of Freedom. If his services are enlisted I am sure he will do much toward solving the problem which faces the minister and the attorney general of British Columbia, for it affects both. The administration of the law rests with British Columbia, but the R.C.M.P. are an agency of the federal parliament charged with the responsibility of carrying out federal laws. They are being used to meet this threat in British Columbia, which places upon the shoulders of the minister a heavy responsibility.
In offering this suggestion I am endeavouring to share that responsibility as one desirous of seeing this problem settled so that no longer will these people, while accepting all the benefits of freedom, whenever they feel like it set out to destroy freedom. They came to this country looking for freedom from persecution. They must be made to realize that we will not have our laws flouted by them at their every whim. In that spirit, and in a desire to see that the criminal law shall not be evaded and circumvented by these people, with the inevitable lessening of public support for law enforcement, I advance this suggestion to the minister knowing what this man can do, having in mind the experience we in Saskatchewan have had with Mr. Wright over a period of fifteen or eighteen years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have one other suggestion to offer, which I believe deserves the attention of parliament. There is no more serious matter in our country today than the matter of drunken driving. In view of the fact that hundreds of people are being killed each year through the negligence of drunken drivers, I feel that the amendments to our criminal law should include some reference to this matter with a view to tightening up the law. Some time ago I asked the minister

Criminal Code
whether he intended to bring in any such amendment. On May 3, 1950, at page 2119, he informed the house and the country that the government did not intend at this session to bring in any amendments to the law with respect to drunken drivers.
Let us view the situation dispassionately. Some 1,800 Canadians are killed each year in motor accidents. Of these some thirty per cent-and this is a reasonable estimate based on the experience of police officers- are killed by drunken drivers. We regard murder as a terrible crime. Drunken drivers kill five times as many Canadians as are murdered. I am not going to place on record a great deal of data on the subject. There was a particularly good article in Maclean's magazine of March 15, 1950, and I am going to summarize what it says. In Canada the accident rate is 12-7 per 100,000. In Sweden, which has taken drastic measures to stop drunken driving, the rate is 4-3. One can determine how serious the situation is by communicating with any crown prosecutor in this country, or with the mounted police. Dr. Joslyn Rogers, the Ontario provincial analyst, has summed up the situation in these words:
The drunk driver's killings and mannings would appal the public if they could be put before people in all their horror. He is the greatest menace we have.
Then I have one other quotation, from Chief Charles Maclver of Winnipeg. Knowing this man as he does, I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will place a good deal of reliance in what he says:
Drunken driving is the No. 1 social problem today. A motorist under the influence of liquor is a potential murderer.
The police chief of Regina has branded it as the gravest social problem with which we have to contend. Yet we go on, year after year, with the criminal code unchanged, the minimum penalty being seven days and the percentage of acquittals particularly high because in many cases the crown is unable to establish guilt. The defence can always be raised that there has been a leak in the pipe in the motor, and the man has suffered from carbon monoxide poisoning, or he has had a heart attack or some other seizure. Perhaps he had a drink three or four hours before, or indeed he may have had a drink only after the police came. Frequently it is urged that the accused smelled of alcohol only because he took a drink after the police came in order to restore his morale.
This problem is not being faced by parliament as it should be. When you recall there are between 500 and 600 Canadians a year, or almost two Canadians a day, killed on the highways by drunken drivers, you can see

that this is a matter which deserves the attention of parliament. The attorney general of British Columbia was under the impression, in an interview he gave on April 28, that amendments to the Criminal Code were being drafted. According to the minister he was in error in that regard.
What should be done? Some would suggest that we increase the penalty. Increasing the penalty very often results in an increase in the number of acquittals. If the minimum penalty is too high the judge or jury will go a long way in order to arrive at a verdict of not guilty when any doubt, however inconsiderable, has been raised. In the explanatory notes of the bill to amend the Customs Act, which was piloted through the house today by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair), the explanation given for reducing the penalties was that the penalties were so high as to constitute an invitation to acquittal. If heavier penalties are not the solution, what other methods are there? I am not here for the purpose of suggesting what methods should be followed. In Sweden, to which I have already made reference, drastic regulations and laws have been in force. According to Maclean's magazine the police of that country have the power to stop a line of cars at any time, on any street or highway, and take blood alcohol tests. Wherever the driver's alcohol percentage goes above the equivalent of one medium drink of whisky he can be sent to jail, and the minimum sentence is two months. That is drastic, and I doubt that such a plan could be accepted under our law.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BREAKING AND ENTERING, FORGERY, ETC.
speechtext: But not too drastic.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BREAKING AND ENTERING, FORGERY, ETC.
speechtext:
I am arguing both sides
of the question, and I can see the point my hon. friend has raised. I know from experience in prosecuting, but more particularly as defence counsel, that heavy minimum penalties defeat the object for which they were established.
What are the alternative suggestions? The alternative suggestion is that chemical tests be provided for under the law, whereby when a person is taken into custody on this charge he may be subjected to either a breath test, blowing his breath into a balloon, or a blood test, which is more drastic, or a test of saliva or urine. Under our law now those tests, if taken, would be illegal; certainly they would not be admissible in evidence. It is not for me to suggest what should be done, but certainly there is no doubt whatever that any person whose blood test showed a reaction of -15 of alcohol is intoxicated to a degree that he is unable to properly operate his motorcar. It is not very long ago that I had

experience in a homicide case; after a drinking party an examination was made of the blood of the deceased, and it was found that the percentage of alcohol was over [DOT] 15. Every medical authority on jurisprudence agrees that at that point a person is in fact unable to form a rational opinion as to the difference between right and wrong, and has lost that control of his motivating capacity as would amount to intoxication.
I feel that something must be done. The number of drunken driver cases is multiplying year by year. Taking the city of Toronto as an example, the figures given for 1945 show that 453 of the drivers in accidents were listed as under the influence or had been drinking; in 1949 the number jumped to 826. In Vancouver there were similar records, and in Winnipeg there was a pronounced increase following the trend across the country. There is no more serious problem today than the problem of dealing with this matter. It is not dealt with today under the section of the Criminal Code. I venture the opinion that if a compulsory blood test or saliva test were provided by law it would afford many persons a defence; and on the other hand it would also provide, for those who escape the just penalty for their wrong, the certainty of conviction in the event that their blood was found to have a percentage of alcohol over -15. Therefore, sir, even at this late date, I bring this matter to the attention of the minister. I believe it is a matter that deserves attention now. Waiting another year means that 600 or more Canadians will be killed because the law is not sufficiently stern, and the enforcement of the law is insufficient to meet the requirements of present-day conditions.
I am one of those whose experience over the years has been largely for the defence. Nevertheless, I believe there is no section of the criminal law that is more evaded and circumvented than the provision against drunken driving. Indeed, as the law is today, there is nothing of a deterrent in the possibility of receiving a sentence of seven days in jail when any person desiring to break the law must realize that the possibility of conviction is next to nothing. However uncertain a person may be, however much he may smell of liquor, however terrible the accident in which he has been involved, there are in the law as it stands today so many loopholes-placed there not by the accused but by parliament-that I feel it should be strengthened. And parliament should not wait one year longer.
I am not going to deal with the phases peculiar to the provinces; but what a farce it is, with those who are convicted generally
Criminal Code
receiving the minimum of seven days, then in a matter of a few weeks getting their cars back again-
