And they are once again placed in possession of an instrument which is as dangerous as or more dangerous than a gun in the hands of many, to go forth with little more danger of a heavier penalty in the event that they again commit an offence, when the penalty becomes thirty days.
Not long ago I saw an example of the results of drunken driving. If the law were made really effective, no one would need to fear anything but his own inclination to be a potential killer. But certainly we in this parliament should see to it that something is done similar to what is today being done in the United States, where in thirty-five states the law is now enforced by means of blood, saliva and breath tests. At any rate, if the minister is afraid that a blood test is too drastic a measure, certainly there is nothing drastic about a breath test. There is no reason why an accused should be unwilling to submit to it.
These are three suggestions which, I submit, deserve attention now. Summarizing them, they are: First, let us stop penalizing anyone for inability to pay a fine. Second, let us do what we can to meet this threat to the enforcement agencies, the challenge to law and its enforcement, to which the Sons of Freedom are constantly subjecting our criminal law. Third, let us make the law inescapable to drunken drivers. If we reduce the death rate within one year by thirty-five per cent-as was the case in at least ten American states-from killings by drunken drivers, we certainly shall have done something worth while; for even if we do no better than that, we save in the next year in Canada two hundred Canadians who have a right to live, and who are asking parliament that that right be preserved by a proper change in the law.

Mr. Chairman, I think if there were no part III in the act the minister would be introducing part III at this time if he were performing his duty. What part III provides is a special procedure to prevent the possession of weapons and liquor in the neighbourhood of public works where such things may be dangerous. Surely this is a step that does not require elaboration at a time like this when sabotage of our great electrical plants would be the very first act of those who would seek to destroy the economy of the country. If we had no such provision in the act I would imagine that what those who are aware of the kind of threat existing in different parts of the world today might well seek to have introduced into the act would be a provision which would make it possible for the government to declare that in the neighbourhood of certain vital public works there should be no arms or alcohol. This section can deal with the type of public works where one or two men can put hundreds or thousands of people out of work simply by the sabotage of these great producing enterprises.
This is not just the sweeping away of dead legislation. It is a bald statement to us, without any supporting evidence, that a section which has not been used for a long time should be brushed aside and made ineffective at the very time that it may conceivably be most useful. One of the most remarkable things about the last war was that through the effectiveness of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the intelligence branches of our military services no major act of sabotage succeeded in this country. We must remember, however, that at that time we were fighting an enemy which had no effective fifth column in Canada. Today the only possible enemy that Canada faces is one with a highly organized fifth column about which the government will do nothing effective. We need a law such as would make it possible for the government to deal with these people if a situation should arise short of war when these traitors to Canada might decide that the time had come for them to cause trouble by interfering with the operation of our great electrical plants, waterways, or anything of that kind that is vital to the development and maintenance of the economy of Canada.

The minister has given no reason for the repeal of part III except to say that it has not been used for many years, and then only in connection with the Hudson Bay railway. Today we see a situation with which we were never confronted before, a situation in which it may be necessary for the government to have the power to take immediate action to deal with those who are openly opposed to the survival of our economy and free system. I would say that if we did not have part III in the act today we should now be advocating it, and I hope the minister will immediately drop the proposal to repeal it and to carry out the other repeals associated with it.

Mr. Chairman, I think my friend is suffering from a complete delusion if he thinks that part III ever had or now has any remote connection with sabotage. The presence of part III in the act is easily explicable. It was put there for the purpose of preventing the consumption of liquor and the possession of weapons in mining and railway camps in order to preserve peace in such places. In a sense it was an imposition to that extent upon the workmen engaged there. It has been found since 1928 that the ordinary provisions of the Criminal Code for the maintenance of law and order are quite sufficient for the purpose of maintaining law and order in such camps, and having regard to the fact that there has never been any occasion, in spite of the large amount of public works under construction since 1928, to proclaim this particular part of the code, there seemed to be no purpose in continuing it.
With my hon. friend's sentiments concerning the prevention of sabotage I would be the first in this house to agree. Certainly I think we should prevent sabotage, but that has nothing to do with part III. In the experience of the law officers of the crown, not those of the Department of Justice but the departments of the attorneys general of the various provinces, part III has not had to be invoked or proclaimed since 1928, nearly twenty-five years ago. They have found no difficulty in maintaining law and order in camps of this sort under the ordinary provisions of the Criminal Code. That being so it is considered wise now to drop it. The method of dealing with sabotage comes under an entirely different branch of the law, and on the proper occasion we shall be glad to go in great detail into the question of the adequacy of the provisions now available to prevent sabotage.

My point is that at this time, far from doing anything that would make it easier to have weapons around any public works, we should be strengthening the law. Let us recognize one thing that we have not been prepared to recognize. Rifles and shotguns, no matter what other purpose they may have, are sporting weapons and are used for that purpose. In reply to my hon. friend, I may say that this amendment was approved by the conference of commissioners on uniformity of legislation in Canada at their 48th meeting. This is a conference on which there are represented all of the departments of the attorneys general of the various provinces of Canada and the federal Department of Justice. They are supposed to be experts in their field. In their view the amendment is advisable. In addition to the awkwardness to which the explanatory note on section 6 of the bill refers, the explanatory note says:
Sections four hundred and sixty-eight, four hundred and sixty-nine and four hundred and seventy specify over forty separate instances of forgery. It is unnecessary and cumbersome to particularize in this manner and the three sections have therefore been combined into one.
In other words, I think my hon. friend would agree that the prosecutor in these cases is, by the nature of the present law, called upon in the indictment to specify which particular one of the forty different varieties of forgery is the one involved in that particular case. Then if he does not bring along evidence to support that particular kind of forgery, there are certain handicaps which

flow back upon the prosecution. By this group of experts it was thought that it was advisable to do away with all of these forty varieties and to have just one crime of forgery which would be applicable to any type of forgery at all.
Another of the difficulties that arise here is that under one of these sections the person convicted could get life imprisonment, under another section he could get fourteen years, and under another he could get seven years. If therefore you picked on one of the forty varieties that happened to be under the life imprisonment section, and all that you could prove was one that was under the fourteen years section, a quite unnecessary hiatus was created just by the terms of the legislation. It is in order to avoid all that and to simplify the criminal law that the conference of commissioners on uniformity of legislation in Canada recommended this amendment.

Remembering that once particulars are given they become part of the charge, you find that you are right back where you are now, with the various divisions which are named. It is all right to say that there are forty different kinds of forgery; there might be more. in breach of the section because the prosecution had set out the particular kind of forgery that he was committing.
I am going to agree with the minister in this. I wish we could simplify things. But I am much worried that by trying to simplify them, in setting out the sections of the Criminal Code, we are not succeeding in doing so. I speak not as an authority but certainly with some experience in these matters. I have convicted many people of forgery. Fortunately, on the other side of the picture, I have had the odd one who was perhaps not convicted. But I know this. Any lawyer in the world who was defending someone on a general charge of forgery, and who would proceed without having the most exact particulars, should have his gown taken from him and should never again be allowed to defend anybody in any court whatever.
However, as always here, we are largely in the hands of the minister who has been advised by various persons in the various provinces in Canada. But the fact that a man is an attorney general-and I speak from experience-does not mean that he knows anything about the criminal law. Let us stick to the practical situation. That is just what it amounts to. I can remember what happened in certain cases. Let us take a charge of conspiracy, under the section dealing with conspiracy, which had to do with prices and so on. I went through two or three courts two or three times to find out, and I had to draw those particulars; I was on the prosecuting side. It was a difficult job; and as has been said by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll), our experience is that the courts will always grant particulars. They always should. Why? Because the liberty of the subject is at stake, and he is entitled to know, to the last detail and comma, what it is the crown intends to prove against him. I have excellent support in the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, but I hate to put myself up against the so-called experts, and I do not use that word derisively at all. It is all right to sit back, but when you get down there in front of that judge and jury, I know what happens. You give particulars. The minister had something to say about the different penalties. Let us assume that the forgery is of the type where a crown document or something of that kind is forged. Of course the most severe penalty should follow. No one has been called in, and I am suggesting that the provision whereby a justice can send a person to a mental institution for thirty days, for examination, would seem to be placing a great deal of power in his hands.
If the section read, "when on the evidence of a competent authority" or something of that kind, it might be understood that such power could be given to a magistrate. But there is no mention about examination, or anyone being called in. It refers only to his opinion, and that seems to be giving the magistrate a great deal of power.

I believe there is some merit in the point raised by the hon. member. But the man would be remanded for observation; it is not as though he made a finding as to sanity. throughout the whole of Canada, but certainly in some parts of it, the term "jail" or "place of confinement" includes mental institutions. That is the only place to which a person of this kind would be admitted.
Use is made of the word "certify" rather generally in respect of people who are mentally ill. Then, when a person is charged, a magistrate can act only on the advice of two physicians. That is the only way in which even the wildest lunatic can be sent to a mental institution, which is a place of confinement. Then he can be released only on an attorney general's warrant.
I quite agree with the hon. member for Lanark that to have a situation such as he has described, wherein a justice of the peace may do something as a result of his opinion, and without prescribing that there shall be evidence from which he could form such an opinion, is carrying things altogether too far,

Criminal Code
and putting too much power in the hands of a man who, honest as he may be, perhaps is not trained to understand insanity.
We know that insanity is a most peculiar ailment. It has never yet been defined satisfactorily by any psychiatrist in the world. In fact, when I cross-examine a psychiatrist my first question always is: What is insanity? I have asked that question dozens of times, and I have never yet heard one psychiatrist who could answer that simple question in any other way than, "It is a departure from the norm." And then the question comes, "Whose norm-mine, yours or somebody else's?" It does seem to me that before a person can be put away for thirty days some other protection should be given. Remember, those in mental institutions are permitted to see their friends only when the people in charge give permission. Their rules are even more strict than those which prevail in the jails. That is necessarily so, and I am not arguing against it.
I do suggest with the greatest respect however, that some further consideration should be given to this matter. In Alberta we have about eight hundred justices of the peace, and in Ontario I suppose they are numbered in thousands. But to place in the hands of an inexperienced man the power to put you or me away for thirty days-true, in order that we may be examined, which is a splendid thing, but without some evidence that we require examination-seems to me to be going altogether too far in dealing with t>he tenable problem you and I know insanity is these days.

I regret that I have to agree with the hon. members for Calgary West and Lanark, but I like to be frank about these matters. Those of us who have had experience with the justices of the peace in our province-and I think possibly the same applies to Manitoba-have not very much confidence in some of them. Any lawyer who has appeared before them knows the difficulties with which he is faced. The practical effect of the section is simply to give power to a justice of the peace to declare anybody who is a mentally fit person to be remanded to an institution. I do not know why you are introducing the section, but under it a justice of the peace can remand anybody. If the hon. member for Calgary West came before a justice of the peace I could urge that he be examined as to his mentality. He might strenuously object to it. He might say that he did not want a remand and that he was mentally sound, but the justice of the peace could remand him under this section, and keep on remanding him. I rather think the section should stand unless there is some explanation. Frankly I must say that I have

always believed in the system of using magistrates. These men are schooled in law, know their law, and when you come before them you know that, so far as evidence or law is concerned, your client is going to be treated fairly. In the province of Saskatchewan ninety per cent of our justices of the peace never knew any law and never should have been appointed.

Let us assume that a given justice of the peace may have been in error in his reaction to the appearance of the accused, that he wrongly thought that the accused should be subject to examination, and that he wrongly, if you like, remanded him into such custody. The immediate reaction

would be that he would be declared to be perfectly sane, would come back, and the trial would proceed. Actually, as those who have been practising criminal law to a much greater extent than I have know-I do not pretend to be an expert in that field at all-in most cases this is a device which is employed not against the interests of the accused but for his protection. Insanity is a defence that may be raised, and the only way in which he can be found to be in that condition is not by compliance with any law this parliament may pass, because that does not happen to be under our constitutional jurisdiction. It is the provinces which declare what mental diseases shall consist of, and who shall decide as to what they consist of.
At the present time in some provinces persons accused of indictable offences who are appearing before magistrates on preliminary hearing are being remanded into such custody, but they run into this procedural difficulty. It is to cure the procedural difficulty beyond any peradventure that these people- and I mean this in no offensive sense at all -have made a point of studying this matter, in order to discharge their heavy responsibility of coming to an agreement and recommending it for consideration by the Department of Justice, as I am now recommending it for consideration by the House of Commons. After careful study of this matter I seriously recommend the section now before you. If I thought for one moment that the section was susceptible of the interpretation placed upon it by the hon. member for Lanark, the hon. member for Calgary West and the hon. member for Yorkton, I would not think of bringing it before the house.
It seems to me, however, that it is a wise thing to regularize the procedure in preliminary inquiries, and any findings as to mental disease in connection therewith must be carried out by the properly qualified people within the provisions of the provincial statute.

I have been very moderate in my remarks, and if in what I have just said I have made a single misstatement or drawn a wrong inference I hope somebody will tell me. As the hon. member for Yorkton said, we are placing in the hands of an individual the power to put an innocent man away for thirty days. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
I do not believe I can answer the question in quite the simple terms in which the hon. member has put it. The present provisions relating to the commencement of sentences are now found in the Criminal Code itself, section 1019 (2), the

Penitentiary Act, 1939, sections 47 (2) and 49 (4), and the Prisons and Reformatories Act, section 3. These provisions, by reason both of their dispersement and of overlapping, are confusing and it is desirable that such provisions be consolidated in one place. The purpose of the present amendment is to consolidate them all in one place.
Clause 20 accomplishes this by inserting a new section, 1054B in the Criminal Code, and the existing provisions are repealed by sections 17, 22 and 23. Section 20 thus effects a consolidation without making any material change in the present law. It does, however, clear up one point in connection with applications for leave to appeal. In some cases the code confers upon an accused person the right to appeal without leave; for example, in the case of a person convicted on indictment who desires to appeal on a question of law alone. In other cases the code confers a right of appeal subject to obtaining leave of the court of appeal; for example, an appeal from sentence or an appeal on the question of fact alone. Section 1019 (2) now provides that the time during which a convicted person is on bail pending the determination of any appeal, and the time during which he is detained in jail pending the determination of an appeal, shall not count as part of his term of imprisonment. The new section 1054B makes it clear in subsection 5 that an application for leave to appeal is to be considered in the same light in this regard as an appeal itself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: Many representations have been made in previous discussions on this bill that some of the benefits should be extended to other classes of veterans. Since those representations were made I am sure the minister has had time to discuss that matter with his colleagues, perhaps, or anyway to form an opinion. subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: I am sorry that cannot be done; but if the minister has definitely decided upon that and assumes the responsibility for not extending these benefits, then may I say that, in my own personal opinion, we should try to get passed through as soon as possible what benefits are now being offered to the imperials or to the men who are already covered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:

I am pleased that allowances have been made to imperial veterans; but I am particularly anxious to know whether this is the clause under which I should discuss the imperial veterans' widows. I should like to see them afforded the same treatment under the act as Canadian veterans receive.

allied veterans of twenty years' residence in Canada will become eligible under this bill, and will be treated in exactly t'he same way as widows of Canadian veterans.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: And the minister has not deviated at all from his original position, which was that unless the imperial veteran had been alive in Canada for twenty years the widow could not qualify. That is still the position?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: I may be a little dense, but I should like a little more explanation from the minister through you, Mr. Chairman. Probably I have not grasped it as I should have. I have been speaking for my own Legion, and I believe for the Legion of the province of British Columbia. We think that wives of those imperial veterans who resided twenty years in Canada should have the same consideration under this particular act as the Canadian veterans. Some of us have been very fortunate in our marriages; some have not been so fortunate. Some may have been married only nineteen years. We have had so much legal discussion tonight that I have become almost legal-minded. I cannot put my point in legal language; it would be too involved. The point I am trying to make is this. A married veteran may have been in Canada twenty years, but he may have been married for only nineteen years. I want to be corrected in this if I am wrong. I have listened to the hon. member for Lake Centre and a few other hon. members taking part in legal discussions tonight and I am beginning to believe that I am legal-minded, but I am not. My contention is that we want every imperial veteran or a veteran of any other allied country who has resided here for twenty years to be accorded the same treatment under the War Veterans Allowance Act as a Canadian veteran. I think the Legion of British Columbia, and certainly my own branch, believe that the widows of the imperial veterans should have the same treatment as the widows of Canadian veterans. Am I wrong or am I correct in my assumption?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fraser Valley is exactly correct. The benefits accruing in this case flow to the wives or the widows through the veterans. The veteran is the person to be recognized; and the wife of the British or allied veteran in Canada twenty years who may have been married after ten years in Canada, but who

otherwise qualifies, would be eligible if she became a widow just the same as the Canadian-born veteran married ten years ago.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: I regret that some consideration has not been given to widows of those imperial veterans who came here over twenty years ago. I do not want to cite any particular case, but I know of several cases. I know of one case in particular where the veteran came out here in 1922. He lived here for twelve years and then died. He left his wife with small children. She struggled, and through her own efforts raised those children. Now she is denied this pension because she was not fortunate enough to have her husband live for twenty years in this country. I think it is a shame that a case like that has not been given some consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: I agree with the other hon. members who have spoken. There is one question I should like to ask the minister. Why is it that we stick to the twenty years? I do not see any logical reason why it should be twenty years. I think it was because we followed the Old Age Pensions Act which required that a foreigner had to be in this country twenty years before he qualified for an old age pension. In studying the old age pensions acts of other countries I have found that they do not require the same length of time. If an alien enters into any of those countries and takes out citizenship within five years, in most of the countries he qualifies for the old age pension. I do not see any particular reason why we should stick to the twenty years. We are amending the act. It seems to me that a shorter time should be specified, which would permit the widows of those imperial veterans to receive the benefits which their husbands would have received had they been here a certain period of time. I should like the minister to explain why twenty years was selected as the time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS

To answer my hon. friend directly, the reason the twenty years has been taken is that all those who have been interested in this question for the last ten years felt that twenty years was a reasonable period of time. It was a period of time, more or less taken by rule of thumb, that it was felt would 55916-189J
War Veterans Allowance Act be fair. From 1920 to 1930 the greater number of these men came to this country. There were a comparatively small number between 1930 and 1940. Then of course the larger group that has come in since the end of the last war will be for somebody else to worry about some fifteen or twenty years hence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS

I refer to the point that the hon. member for Royal made reference to and the one that the hon. member for Fraser Valley is not clear on. No matter when the imperial veteran married, if he was in this country for twenty years, his wife is eligible; but an imperial veteran may have been in this country for nineteen years and six months and then passed on. His widow is not entitled to this award, although she may have been here all her life. I would like to know how many are affected. I myself think that it is a pretty rank piece of discrimination. I wonder whether the minister has any figures on the number that would be affected. I imagine there are few. I believe the amendments are all right as they are, but there is that one point that sticks out, and there is a lot of resentment over it. subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
This is the section which provides that moneys received under a pension shall not be considered in arriving at a figure for war veterans allowance. Can the minister say what provisions are made in his department for cross-checking between the pensions branch and the veterans allowance branch? On one or two occasions difficulties have arisen in that pension has been increased because the disability of a veteran has become greater; he has received additional money as a result of that increase; at the same time he has been drawing war veterans allowance, but no prompt notification has been sent from the pensions branch to the war veterans allowance board.
The result has been that perhaps a year or eighteen months later the veteran has suddenly been faced with a notification that he has been overpaid. Then of course deductions have been made from his allowance,


and a great deal of suffering has been caused which could have been avoided if there had been some system in the department whereby, the minute a pension was increased, notification had gone to the war veterans allowance board so that the allowance could be adjusted accordingly.
In some cases which have come to my attention veterans have received this increase, have thought they were entitled to it, and did not realize that it was going to affect the war veterans allowance. Then they were faced with a demand for several hundred dollars, perhaps a year or two later.
The income of such a veteran is limited; he can receive only a certain maximum; if he gets part of it in pension, then he gets that much less in war veterans allowance. So when this notification comes he is on a fixed income, and faced with repayment of several hundred dollars. I believe a difficulty of that kind could be avoided by a more efficient exchange of information between these two branches of the minister's department. Have any steps been taken to bring about such an exchange?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: In the planning that is taking place now active steps are under way to obviate the difficulty pointed out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
I have had cases of my own that I have had to look after, affected in much the same way. For instance, a veteran's wife has been faced with sudden and serious illness, and the veteran has been called upon to make payment back, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has said. These sums have been deducted all at once. Still he has to pay doctor and hospital bills.
It is not reasonable that they should be called upon to make these refunds. If a man is entitled to war veterans allowance, it is because he needs it and because he is incapable of earning a full livelihood for his family. He is receiving it owing to the shortening of his life and earning ability through war service. It is most unreasonable to deduct from that man, as has been done in the cases I have had brought (to my attention. His wife might require the expenditure of large sums of money each month for medicinal purposes; yet the veteran all at once has these sums deducted. Further consideration should be given to this.
